details:
What it does and how it works. Heartbeat Telemetry is a health monitoring system that runs on board the spacecraft. As a proof of concept, a Samsung Galaxy Watch (Wear OS) collects heart rate, beat-to-beat intervals for heart rate variability, skin temperature, blood oxygen and ECG, and sends them to an onboard server. The server combines them with NASA data (ISS radiation from RadLab, ISS cabin air from OSDR, and the ISS food menu) and rates each area green, yellow or red against NASA-STD-3001 limits and the astronaut's own baseline, explaining what it means, why it matters in space, and what to do. The app is organized around NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity, and a hostile closed environment. It works without Earth: data is relayed to a flight surgeon console with a realistic communication delay (ISS, Moon or Mars), and red alerts are sent to the surgeon automatically.

Benefits. Astronauts see their own health at a glance on the watch and a dashboard, with plain-language guidance instead of raw numbers. Scheduled tasks (ECG, blood oxygen, a daily mood and stress check-in, meal logging and exercise) earn points, streaks and badges, so taking measurements becomes a habit. The flight surgeon sees the whole crew and receives alerts without anyone having to send them.

Intended impact. On long missions, astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting health changes themselves, because help from Earth arrives late. Heartbeat Telemetry aims to give the crew the information and guidance to act right away, while keeping the ground informed. The same approach could help anyone far from medical care who wears a consumer watch.

How it is creative. The ship comes first and Earth second: every rating is made on board, and the surgeon only ever sees what has crossed the link, delay included. Each status combines NASA limits with the astronaut's own baseline and explains itself. A clearly labeled simulated solar storm, built from the real September 2017 solar event in NASA's RadLab data, shows how an alert travels from the ship to Earth.

Tools, languages, hardware and software. The watch sends its readings to the onboard server over Wi-Fi through an HTTP API. The watch app is written in Kotlin with Compose for Wear OS and the Samsung Health Sensor SDK. The server is built with Node.js and TypeScript (Fastify) and stores data in PostgreSQL, running in a Docker container. The astronaut dashboard and flight surgeon console are built with React (Next.js), with live updates over WebSocket.

Factors we considered. Our goal was a health tracking system that is easy for astronauts to use, and that replicates the space environment as closely as possible with inexpensive equipment. Cost was a deciding factor, so we used consumer-grade hardware together with real NASA mission data to make the system behave as it would on a real spacecraft. We also considered the communication delay, working without an internet connection, battery life on the watch.
